HAND EDIT. Every key of a NoETL playbook (`https://noetl.ai/schema/v2/playbook.schema.json`), as the grammar defines it. Chapters 4–6 teach these keys; the *Taught in* column links to the chapter.

> NoETL playbook grammar (noetl.io/v2), generated from the Rust authoring types in noetl-orchestrate-core 0.1.0. Permissive like the parser (unknown keys are not rejected); `tool.kind` is closed to the kinds this server accepts. Semantic rules (a `start` step, unique step names, existing `next` targets) are enforced by the server's validator, not by this schema.

### CursorClaim

The claim block of a `mode: cursor` loop — a SQL tool that atomically leases a frame of work rows and returns them (its `RETURNING` columns become the per-row `iter.<iterator>` object).

Taught in [Ch. 6.3](ch06-03-loop.md).

| Key | Type | Required | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `auth` | string \| null |  |  | Credential alias for the claim tool. |
| `claim` | string | yes |  | The claim SQL (atomic lease, e.g. `... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED ... RETURNING ...`). |
| `kind` | string |  | `"postgres"` | Tool kind running the claim (default `postgres`). |

### KeychainDef

Keychain entry for credential/token definitions.

Taught in [Ch. 4.4](ch04-04-keychain.md).

| Key | Type | Required | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `allowed_regions` | array of string |  | `[]` | Secrets Wallet Phase 6c — extra regions (besides the entry's own `region`) from which resolution is allowed when `residency` is `strict` or `advisory`.  Empty by default. |
| `auth` | string \| null |  |  | Credential alias used to authenticate to `provider` (e.g. a service account). On a provider that authenticates by ambient identity (GCP Workload Identity), this is unused. |
| `auto_renew` | boolean |  | `false` | Auto-renew flag. |
| `credential` | string \| null |  |  | Credential reference. |
| `map` | map of string \| null |  |  | Output-key → secret-reference map. Each value is a secret-path template (rendered against the workload at resolution time); the resolved entry is the object `{ <key>: <secret-value>, ... }` — the "auth object as a map" shape. Absent for single-value entries. |
| `name` | string | yes |  | Keychain entry name. |
| `no_broker_fallback` | boolean |  | `false` | Secrets Wallet Phase 6e — opt-out for the cross-region broker fallback.  When `true`, a strict-mode residency denial bubbles up as `ResidencyViolation` even if a broker is configured for the entry's region — used for credentials whose policy says "this data physically cannot leave its home region, full stop." Default `false` (broker fallback honoured when registered). |
| `provider` | string \| null |  |  | Secret-source backend that resolves this entry: `gcp` (Google Secret Manager), `aws`, `azure`, `vault`, `k8s`. When set, the server-side keychain resolver fetches the value(s) from this provider on a cache miss (Secrets Wallet Phase 3b). `None` means the entry is supplied by other means (pre-registered credential, minted token). |
| `region` | string \| null |  |  | Secrets Wallet Phase 6a — home region of this secret (e.g. `us-east-1`, `europe-west4`).  When set, the resolver passes it to the chosen `crate::secrets::SecretProvider`: AWS uses it as the regional endpoint host; Azure / Vault use it for vault / cluster routing; GCP uses it as part of the resource id.  `None` falls back to the server's `NOETL_SERVER_REGION` env.  Per `agents/rules/safety.md`, the region is a routing hint, not a secret — public-safe. |
| `residency` | Residency |  | `"none"` | Secrets Wallet Phase 6c — residency policy.  Controls whether a server in a different region than this entry's `region` is allowed to resolve it.  See `crate::secrets::residency::Residency`. |
| `scope` | string \| null |  |  | Scope type. |
| `token_type` | string \| null |  |  | Token type. |

### LoopMode

Loop execution mode.

Taught in [Ch. 6.3](ch06-03-loop.md).

One of:

- "sequential" \| "parallel"
- "cursor": Claim-based work-distribution loop (noetl/ai-meta#100).  Instead of a fixed `in:` collection, the orchestrator repeatedly runs the `loop.cursor.claim` SQL to lease a frame of work rows, fans out the step body per claimed row, then re-claims — until the claim returns zero rows (drained).  Honors the Rust execution model: the claim runs as a normal postgres tool command on a worker; no long-lived worker.

### NextArc

Arc specification for v10 next router format. Canonical format: next.arcs\[\].when for conditional routing (Petri-net arcs).

Taught in [Ch. 6.1](ch06-01-next-and-routers.md).

| Key | Type | Required | Default | Description |

| `set` | object \| null |  |  | Arc-level variable mutations to apply to execution context before dispatching the downstream step.  Mirrors Python's `set:` on arcs. Scope-prefixed keys (`ctx.x`, `iter.x`, `step.x`) are stripped to the bare key; bare keys and unknown-scope dotted keys are written as-is.  Values are Jinja2 templates rendered against the producing step's completion context before being applied. |
| `step` | string | yes |  | Target step name. |
| `when` | string \| null |  |  | Transition guard expression (Jinja2). Evaluated by server after step completion. |

### NextSpec

Next step specification - supports multiple formats for compatibility.

Taught in [Ch. 6.1](ch06-01-next-and-routers.md).

One of:

- array of CanonicalNextTarget: List of step targets with optional `when` (legacy canonical): a sequence of `{ step, when?, args? }` maps.
- array of string: List of bare step names.
- string: Single step name.
- NextRouter: Canonical v10 router format: `{ spec: { mode: ... }, arcs: \[...\] }` — a map. Declared last so a sequence never deserializes into it positionally (see the type-level note above).

### PipelineItem

One item in a pipeline.  Untagged so serde tries each variant in declaration order and picks the first that decodes.

Taught in [Ch. 5.2](ch05-02-ordered-tool-list.md).

One of:

- ToolSpec: Flat shape: `{ name: "label", kind: "python", code: "...", ... }`. The pipeline-item label lives in the `name` field; the rest of the fields are an inline `ToolSpec`.  Stored via `ToolSpec.extra` (the `#\[serde(flatten)\] HashMap` catch-all), so no schema change is needed on ToolSpec itself.
- map of ToolSpec: Nested shape: `{ "label": { kind: "python", code: "...", ... } }`. Single-key map — the key is the label, the value is the spec.

### Residency

Residency policy for a `KeychainDef` — part of the playbook model, so it lives in the core with the rest of the types (noetl/ai-meta#108).  The server's `secrets::residency` module re-exports this enum and holds the region-check *logic* (which needs server-only deps); the enum itself is pure data.

Taught in [Ch. 4.4](ch04-04-keychain.md).

One of:

- "none": No check; resolution proceeds regardless of server region. Back-compat default for entries without an explicit policy.
- "advisory": Check but proceed on mismatch — observability without enforcement. Used during the migration window before flipping to `strict`.
- "strict": Fail-closed on mismatch; resolution short-circuits before any provider call (the server maps this to an `AppError::ResidencyViolation`).

### ToolKind

Supported tool kinds.

Taught in [Ch. 5.1](ch05-01-tool-kinds.md).

One of:

- "http" \| "postgres" \| "duckdb" \| "ducklake" \| "python" \| "workbook" \| "playbook" \| "playbooks" \| "secrets" \| "iterator" \| "container" \| "script" \| "snowflake" \| "transfer" \| "snowflake_transfer" \| "gcs" \| "gateway" \| "nats" \| "shell" \| "artifact" \| "noop" \| "task_sequence" \| "rhai"
- "subscription": Bounded-drain message subscription poll (NATS / Pub/Sub / Kafka). noetl/ai-meta#90 Phase 1 — dispatched generically by the worker through the noetl-tools registry; the server only needs to accept the kind so playbook validation passes.
- "wasm": Compiled WASM plug-in (noetl/ai-meta#105). The step's tool carries `plugin: { path, version, entry? }` and an optional `input` (the server canonicalises it to `args`, which becomes the plug-in's input bytes as JSON). `path` is a string, `version` an integer, `entry` the guest export to call (default `run`). The server only accepts the kind; the worker's `wasm-plugin` dispatcher loads the module from the catalog, runs it and flushes its capability intents.
